fields.features_heading: What Makes an Interior Design Style Quiz Work
fields.features_subheading: Describe the quiz in one prompt. Emergent builds it, then changes whatever you describe next.
fields.feature_1:
Options mapped to styles, scored by count

Name the styles you want as results and Emergent drafts questions whose options each point to one style. The style picked most often wins, and you reword any question by prompt.
fields.feature_2:
A result screen that leads somewhere

Each style ends on its own screen: the name, a short read on the preference, and the next step you choose, such as a gallery, a booking link, or a product list from your catalog.
fields.feature_3:
Every finished quiz lands in your table

Answers, the result, and the finish time are saved as one row in a database you own. Filter rows by style before a season starts, or export the whole table whenever you need it.
fields.feature_4:
An email step you can turn off

Ask for an email before the result screen, or skip the gate entirely. When a finished quiz names a budget over a line you set, the app sends a Slack or email alert the same hour.
fields.feature_5:
Built for a phone, with no response caps

Visitors answer one screen at a time with a progress bar, and the quiz keeps accepting entries past any count, because Emergent puts no response caps on surveys or quizzes.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain now, your code later

Host the quiz on your own domain, included in Emergent and billed in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and change anything in it directly.

fields.howto_title: How to Make an Interior Design Style Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan an interior design style quiz, map every answer to a style, and build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the styles your results will name
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Decide what happens after the result
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask about rooms people live in
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Keep every option concrete and even
fields.howto_step_1_des: Name the result styles first and keep to 4 to 6, because every question needs one option per style. Pick styles you can serve afterward: a gallery you can fill, products you can tag, or a finish package you sell.
fields.howto_step_2_des: A result screen that only names a style wastes the visit. Give each style a next step before you write questions: a consultation form, tagged products, or a guide signup. The destination decides which intake fields the quiz should collect.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask what someone keeps, not what they admire in photos. A question about the sofa they bought, the shelf they cleared, or the finish they chose reads taste better than one about dream homes, and it keeps every option concrete.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tie each option to one style and word it as a real object, so a visitor picks between things instead of adjectives. If a test run never lands on one style, its options read as the safe middle choice; rewrite them.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Ask for room and budget last
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put one or two intake questions after the style questions, where finishing is close. A designer needs the room and a budget line; a store needs an email at most. Cut any field you will not read this month.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test every path before you share it
fields.howto_step_6_des: Take the quiz once per style, answering for that style on purpose, and check each result screen, the saved row, and any alert you set up. Fix the wording wherever you hesitated: the place you paused is where a visitor quits.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Put the quiz where decisions start
fields.howto_step_7_des: Link it from the consultation page, the signup form, or the booking confirmation rather than a blog footer. Watch the results table for 2 weeks and compare styles: if one result never appears, revisit its options before you change the page.

faq_plan.q: What is an interior design style quiz?
faq_plan.a: An interior design style quiz is a short set of questions about the rooms, furniture, and finishes you like, scored so your answers point to one named style. The quiz on this page asks eight questions and names one of five styles, from Japandi to Bohemian.

faq_plan.q: How do I create an interior design style quiz?
faq_plan.a: Start by naming the result styles, then write one prompt that says what each result should lead to. Emergent's AI survey builder drafts questions with one option per style, builds the result screens, and saves every finished quiz to a database you own. Publish it and share the link.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should an interior design style quiz have?
faq_plan.hint: What's my interior design style quiz buzzfeed?
faq_plan.a: Keep it to 6 to 10 style questions. With fewer, a single tie decides too many results; with more, the quiz takes longer than the choice deserves. The quiz on this page uses eight and asks for no contact details.

faq_plan.q: Which styles should an interior design style quiz offer as results?
faq_plan.hint: What's my interior design style quiz free?
faq_plan.a: Offer 4 to 6 styles your business can act on, such as Japandi, Coastal, Mid-Century, Traditional, and Bohemian for a design studio. A general style quiz can mix fashion and decor. Keep this one inside rooms: every result should point to a gallery, a package, or products you carry.

faq_plan.q: Should an interior design style quiz require an email to see the result?
faq_plan.a: Only if you will send something specific to each style. Run one version with the email step and one without, then compare finished quizzes in your table. If you keep it, place it after the last style question and say what the email will contain.

faq_plan.q: How do you score an interior design style quiz when answers split between two styles?
faq_plan.a: Count picks per style and show the one with the most. Decide the tie rule in advance: the quiz on this page gives a tie to the style listed first. A results page can also name the runner-up, since a Japandi and Coastal split is useful to a designer.

faq_plan.q: Can the same setup run other quizzes besides an interior design style quiz?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Any quiz where each option points to one result works the same way, whether the results are decor styles or the animals in a spirit animal quiz. Emergent builds the result screens and the table from your prompt, and you change either one by describing the change.

faq_plan.q: How do designers use interior design style quiz results with new clients?
faq_plan.a: They read the result before the first meeting and bring examples in that style instead of starting from a blank questionnaire. Ask for the room and budget in the same quiz. The result, the scope, and the money then arrive on one record.

faq_plan.q: Can I offer an interior design style quiz free to visitors without a login?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Leave out sign-in and contact fields, and anyone with the link can take the quiz and see the result. Emergent is free to start, and the free tier covers building and publishing the quiz.

faq_plan.q: Can two people compare their interior design style quiz results?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if the quiz asks each person for a shared code that links both results to one record. Couples furnishing a home can see where their styles overlap, the same way a friendship quiz lines up two people's answers. Each result still saves as its own row.

quiz.title: What Is Your Interior Design Style?
quiz.intro: Eight questions about the rooms you live in and the things you keep. Your result names the interior design style your answers lean toward, with ideas to build on it.

options.text: A low oak frame with linen cushions
A slipcovered sofa in white cotton
A walnut-legged sofa with tight cushions
A rolled-arm sofa in a deep velvet
A deep sofa piled with mismatched pillows

questions.text: Pick the floor you want under your feet.

options.text: Pale wood with nothing on it
Whitewashed planks and a jute rug
Warm teak with a geometric rug

Layered vintage rugs, edge to edge

questions.text: What sits on your coffee table right now, or would in your ideal room?

options.text: One ceramic bowl and nothing else
A woven tray with a few shells
A sculptural lamp and a design book
A stack of hardbacks and a silver box

options.text: Warm white, oat, and charcoal

Mustard, olive, and walnut brown

A rattan pendant
A brass globe chandelier
A crystal chandelier
A cluster of beaded lanterns

options.text: Behind closed doors, out of sight
In baskets along an open shelf
In a long credenza with sliding doors
In a glass-front cabinet, on display
Out where you can see and use them

options.text: A handmade stoneware vase
A weathered driftwood mirror
A molded plywood side chair
An oil landscape in a gilt frame

results.title: Japandi
results.description: Your answers lean toward calm rooms with few objects, pale wood, and natural fabrics. Start with one low, well-made piece per room, keep surfaces clear, and add texture through linen, paper, and stoneware instead of color.

results.title: Coastal
results.description: Your answers lean toward light, airy rooms in sand and soft blue, with woven textures underfoot and overhead. Build on washable white fabrics, rattan, and jute, and keep window treatments light enough to let the daylight in.

results.title: Mid-Century
results.description: Your answers lean toward warm wood, clean lines, and furniture on slim legs. Anchor a room with one walnut or teak piece, add a sculptural lamp, and bring in mustard or olive through a rug or a single chair.

results.title: Traditional
results.description: Your answers lean toward rich colors, dark wood, and pieces with some history. Pair a classic sofa with patterned rugs and lined drapes, and keep the room balanced with matching lamps and framed art.

results.title: Bohemian
results.description: Your answers lean toward layered, collected rooms full of plants, pattern, and travel finds. Start with a warm base of terracotta and green, layer rugs and textiles, and let the things you love stay out on display.

plan.angle: The top 10 is consumer quizzes from designer blogs, a trade association, a TV network, and retail showrooms: every one ends at a style name and an email gate. None lets the visitor build the quiz itself. This page does both: a playable interior design style quiz on the page, then four businesses that put results to work in ways the top 10 never shows: a design studio that opens its first client call at the result instead of a blank questionnaire, a home builder that maps results to its finish packages, a decor subscription box that packs each box against the subscriber's style profile, and a decor newsletter that sends its gift guide in one version per style. Every result lands in a database the owner keeps, with no response cap.
